title: Temporal Association Between Reported Use of Psychoactive Substances and Cognitive Function in Individuals With Multiple Sclerosis.
abstract: The study aimed to examine same-day within-person associations between psychoactive substance use and cognitive function in people with multiple sclerosis (MS) using ecological momentary assessment. This secondary analysis used data collected over 14 days from people with MS. Community. Ambulatory adults with MS (N=257). Not applicable. Participants completed daily ecological momentary assessment via smartphone, reporting use of psychoactive substances (alcohol, cannabis, opioids, nicotine, and caffeine) and perceived cognitive function. Objective cognitive performance was assessed using the Dot Memory Test (working memory) and Symbol Search Tests (processing speed). Of the 274 enrolled participants, 257 completed the 14-day monitoring phase, yielding over 14,000 assessments with >76% completion across measures. At the between-person level, no significant associations were observed between average substance use and cognitive outcomes. However, within-person analyses revealed that caffeine use was associated with better perceived cognitive function (B=-3.31; P<.001) and faster processing speed (B=-32.58; P=.01). Cannabis use predicted worse perceived cognitive function (B=3.38; P=.049) and alcohol use was linked to poorer working memory performance (B=0.05; P=.02). No significant within-person effects were found for nicotine or opioid use. Caffeine may produce short-term cognitive benefits, whereas cannabis and alcohol are related to negative cognitive effects. Findings highlight the importance of developing personalized, evidence-based guidance for people with MS who may consume psychoactive substances for symptom management, recreation, or other reasons.
fulltext:
Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by inflammatory demyelination and neurodegeneration within the central nervous system.1 As one of the most prevalent neurological disorders affecting young adults, MS typically manifests between the ages of 20 and 40, with nearly 1 million individuals diagnosed in the United States.2 MS presents with a diverse array of symptoms, including physical symptoms such as pain,3 fatigue,4 and spasticity,5 as well as psychological challenges such as anxiety and depression.6 Furthermore, cognitive impairments, particularly deficits in memory function and processing speed, often emerge early in the disease course and progressively worsen over time.7,8 The cumulative burden of these symptoms significantly impacts the quality of life of individuals living with MS.9 Despite advancements in MS research, effective pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatment options for symptom management remain limited.10
Given that clinician-prescribed treatments may not fully manage symptoms, efforts to self-manage symptoms are commonly observed in individuals with MS. Self-management of symptoms may include consumption of psychoactive substances in a manner that is similar to how the general public may consume a caffeine drink to combat fatigue or nicotine to manage stress. Cannabis11–13 and opioids14 are commonly used to alleviate pain, spasticity, and sleep disturbances in people with MS. Alcohol is frequently consumed to reduce stress and enhance mood.15 Caffeine has been shown to have positive effects on mobility and quality of life in MS.16
While some psychoactive substances have shown therapeutic potential in MS — such as cannabis for pain and spasticity relief13 — there is growing concern regarding their potential inadvertent adverse effects. Substance use, such as alcohol and cannabis, has been linked to worsened depression17,18 and accelerated cognitive decline.19,20 Neuroimaging studies in people with substance use disorders have revealed significant neurobiological alterations, including structural and functional abnormalities in the brain.21 Different substances appear to exert distinct cognitive effects. Cannabis use has shown between-person association with poorer cognitive performance20,22,23 and perceived cognitive function,11 whereas caffeine consumption has shown cognitive benefits.24
However, previous research on MS has primarily focused on cannabis and caffeine, leaving gaps in understanding the cognitive impact of other commonly used substances such as alcohol, nicotine, and opioids. Additionally, most studies have relied on cross-sectional designs, which provide insights into the between-person associations between substance use and cognitive function (e.g., people who use cannabis tend to exhibit worse cognitive function compared to those who do not), but fail to elucidate the temporal within-person associations (e.g., when people use substances, do they tend to have worse or better than usual cognitive function immediately or shortly after?). Therefore, the present study aims to investigate the impact of substance use on the subsequent cognitive function in people with MS by employing ecological momentary assessment (EMA) to capture real-time self-reported substance use and subjective cognitive function, and ambulatory cognitive tests to assess real-time cognitive performance. We hypothesize that central nervous system depressants (i.e., alcohol, cannabis, opioids) will be associated with subsequent declines in perceived cognitive function and cognitive performance, whereas stimulants (i.e., caffeine, nicotine) will be associated with improvements in perceived cognitive function and cognitive performance. By examining these relationships, this study seeks to enhance our understanding of the within-person association between cognitive function and substance use in MS, informing future clinical guidelines to support cognitive health in this population.
Methods
Participants
This secondary analysis used microlongitudinal data from a 14-day study on cognitive changes in MS.25 To participate, individuals had to meet the following criteria: age ≥18, fluent English, confirmed MS diagnosis, and ability to walk ≥50% of the time (with or without aid). Exclusion criteria included MS relapse in the past 30 days or inability to use study tools.
Data collection
Following approval from the University of Michigan’s medical institutional review board, participants were recruited from three research sites: the University of Michigan (Ann Arbor, MI), Wayne State University (Detroit, MI), and the University of Washington (Seattle, WA). Recruitment occurred across three U.S. research sites via registries, clinical referrals, and outreach. After phone screening, eligible individuals completed a baseline lab visit (up to 2.5 hours) for informed consent and baseline assessment, followed by 14 days of EMA and cognitive testing at four time points daily (morning, midday, evening, and bedtime) using a study-provided smartphone. Data were collected from May 2022 to April 2024. This manuscript describes the initial data collection (first laboratory visit and 14-day ambulatory monitoring period).
Measures
Laboratory visit measures
Participants completed a self-reported survey of demographics such as age, sex, race, education, and employment. In addition, clinical characteristics include MS subtype, years since diagnosis, and self-reported disability (Patient Determined Disease Steps [PDDS]).26
Ambulatory Measures
Substance use was assessed by asking “Since the last assessment, did you consume (check all that apply): 1) alcohol; 2) caffeine; 3) nicotine; 4) cannabis; 5) opioids; 6) none of the above?” Perceived cognitive function27 was assessed using three visual analog scale items (0–100), with higher scores indicating greater cognitive difficulties (total score range: 0–300). For example, participants rated, “RIGHT NOW…How foggy is your thinking?” (Figure 1). Higher scores indicate worse perceived cognitive function. For objective cognitive function measures, the Dot Memory Test and the Symbol Search Test were administered to assess processing speed and working memory, respectively.28 For the Dot Memory Test, each trial consisted of three phases: (1) encoding, where participants viewed and memorized the location of three red dots on a 5×5 grid for 3 seconds; (2) distraction, where they completed a visual search task (identifying F’s among E’s); and (3) retrieval, where they placed the red dots on a blank grid in the remembered locations. Accuracy and reaction time were recorded, and only sessions with ≥70% accuracy were included. For the Symbol Search Test, participants viewed four symbol pairs at the top of the screen and two symbol pairs at the bottom. They selected the pair at the bottom that matched one of the top pairs as quickly as possible. Each task was administered four times daily. Both measures have demonstrated strong psychometric properties across diverse populations, including people with MS28,29, and showed excellent reliability in the current sample, with intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.99 across all cognitive tasks.
Data analyses
Participants’ demographic and clinical characteristics were summarized using descriptive statistics (i.e., means, standard deviations, frequencies, and percentages). Given the nested structure of the data, we employed mixed-effects multilevel modeling (MLM) to examine the temporal within-person association of psychoactive substance use (alcohol, nicotine, caffeine, opioids, and cannabis) with cognitive function. Each substance use variable was dummy coded (0 = no, 1 = yes). In addition, the total number of each substance used per participant was included in the models to capture between-person differences in substance use. After controlling for age, sex, education years, and PDDS, three separate MLM analyses were conducted, each corresponding to a different cognitive measure, to determine whether psychoactive substance use predicts perceived cognitive function, working memory (mean error distance), and processing speed (median response time). In these models, both substance use and cognitive function were assessed at the same timepoint; however, the substance use questionnaire assessed use since the previous evaluation. Therefore, the substance use variable temporally preceded the cognitive outcome, allowing for a naturally lagged interpretation of within-person associations without the need for explicit time-lagged variable construction. To account for potential confounding by time of day (e.g., variations in substance use or cognitive performance across different timepoints), both day and four EMA timepoints were included as covariates in all models. Random intercepts were incorporated to account for individual variability. A first-order autoregressive covariance structure was selected a priori based on the expectation of temporally declining correlation as the data was collected over time, and confirmed as the best-fitting structure compared to alternative specifications using AIC model fit indices. Model parameters were estimated using restricted maximum likelihood. Missing data were retained, as MLM is robust to missing values.30 All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 28.0. A power analysis was performed using the GLIMMPSE software,31 with a sample size of 257 and an alpha level of 0.05, which indicated that the study had greater than 80% power to detect statistically significant within-person effects.
Results
Participants characteristics
Table 1 provides a summary of sample characteristics. Of 274 enrolled people with MS, 257 completed the home monitoring phase. The mean age of participants was 50.9±11.8 years, and 77.4% were female. Most of the participants were White (73.1%) and had relapsing-remitting (83.2%), with an average disease duration of 16.4 years. Across the study, participants could complete up to 56 assessments each, totaling 14,392 possible data points. Completion rates were high: 77.6% for substance use, 77.2% for perceived cognition, 76.5% for the Dot Memory Test, and 76.1% for the Symbol Search Test. Caffeine was the most commonly used substance (83.7%), followed by alcohol (49.4%), cannabis (28.8%), nicotine (14.4%), and opioids (8.2%). Among users, the median frequency of reported use (as a percentage of assessments) was highest for nicotine (50.0%) and most variable across individuals.
Between-person association between psychoactive substance use and cognitive function
MLM analyses indicated that, at the between-person level, there were no significant associations between psychoactive substance use and cognitive function (Table 2). Individuals who reported higher average use of substances across the monitoring period did not differ in either perceived or objective cognitive performance compared to those who used less.
Within-person temporal association between psychoactive substance use and cognitive function
Table 2 presents the within-person associations between psychoactive substance use and later cognitive function. Caffeine use was associated with better perceived cognitive performance; participants reported fewer cognitive difficulties following caffeine consumption (B = −3.31, p < .01). Follow-up analyses indicated that this association held across all three items assessing perceived cognitive function. In contrast, cannabis use was associated with increased self-reported cognitive difficulties (B = 3.38, p < .05), particularly with reports of slowed thinking (B = 1.66, p = .02). Alcohol, nicotine, and opioid use were not significantly associated with perceived cognitive function. Caffeine use was also linked to improved processing speed, reflected by faster response times on the Symbol Search Test (B = −32.58, p = .01). A post-hoc analysis found a significant interaction between momentary caffeine use and individuals’ average caffeine use (B = −3.12, p = .04), indicating that the beneficial effect of caffeine on processing speed was more pronounced among individuals with lower average caffeine consumption. Alcohol use predicted poorer working memory performance, as indicated by greater error distance on the Dot Memory Test (B = 0.05, p = .02). No significant associations were observed for nicotine, cannabis, or opioid use with objective cognitive function.
Discussion
This study investigated the temporal association between psychoactive substance use and cognitive function in people with MS. To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine within-person relationships across multiple substances in this population. Our findings indicate that caffeine and alcohol were the most commonly used substances, followed by cannabis, while nicotine and opioid use were infrequent. Notably, caffeine consumption showed a within-person association with better perceived cognitive function and faster processing speed, although it did not significantly affect working memory. In contrast, alcohol use was associated with subsequent declines in working memory, and cannabis use was linked to increased perceived cognitive difficulties. Nicotine and opioid use showed no significant within-person temporal associations with cognitive function.
While no substances demonstrated significant between-person associations with cognitive function in our study, prior research investigating between-person associations suggests that long-term substance use can have cognitive effects. For instance, prolonged cannabis use affects multiple cognitive domains such as processing speed, working memory, and executive function, among people with MS compared to non-users.20 Similarly, chronic alcohol and opioid use are associated with cognitive impairment in the general population.32,33 Conversely, moderate caffeine intake has been linked to better verbal memory performance in people with MS.34 The discrepancy between our findings and previous studies may stem from differences in study design, particularly our short-term EMA approach (14 days), which may not have been sufficient to capture between-person effects. Additionally, we did not assess the duration or dose of substance use, limiting our ability to evaluate its cumulative impact on cognition. It is also important to note that this study did not recruit participants based on their substance use patterns, so our sample likely included a limited number of individuals with habitual or heavy substance use, further reducing our power to detect between-person effects. Future studies that recruit individuals with varying levels of substance use and incorporate detailed substance use characterization will be essential to better understand the cognitive consequences of long-term psychoactive substance use in MS. The significant within-person effects observed for caffeine, alcohol, and cannabis suggest that these substances exert temporary, state-dependent effects on cognitive function in people with MS. Caffeine, a well-established central nervous system stimulant, enhances cognitive performance by blocking adenosine receptors and increasing dopamine and norepinephrine release.35 In healthy populations, caffeine improves alertness and attention,36 and similar effects may extend to individuals with MS. The significant interaction between within- and between-person levels of use suggests that non-habitual caffeine users may experience greater cognitive benefits from caffeine intake, potentially due to increased sensitivity to its stimulant effects. However, the lack of a significant effect on working memory suggests that caffeine’s benefits may be more pronounced in attention-related domains rather than working memory. Future studies exploring various cognitive domains could further clarify caffeine’s role in MS-related cognitive function.
There is limited research on the effects of alcohol consumption on cognitive function in people with MS to compare the findings from this study. However, extensive literature in the general population indicates that excessive alcohol consumption can impair cognitive function.37,38 Alcohol has been shown to disrupt immediate memory and information retrieval,39 which aligns with our finding that alcohol consumption was associated with transient declines in working memory. While occasional alcohol use may have minimal long-term consequences, chronic and excessive alcohol consumption has been related to persistent memory deficits32,40 and structural brain damage, particularly in the hippocampus, hypothalamus, and cerebellum—regions crucial for memory.41,42 These neurotoxic effects may accelerate cognitive decline, particularly in individuals already vulnerable to cognitive impairment, such as those with MS. Given these risks, healthcare providers should assess drinking habits in this population and provide targeted interventions to mitigate potential long-term effects. Notably, research suggests that cognitive dysfunction related to alcohol use can improve with sustained abstinence of over a year.43 Individuals with MS who engage in chronic alcohol use may benefit from tailored guidance that considers clinically meaningful patterns of alcohol consumption. Similar approaches have been proposed in other neurological populations to help reduce alcohol use.44
Our study found that cannabis use in people with MS is associated with increased perceived cognitive difficulties but showed no significant relationship with objective cognitive measures. Cannabis exerts its effects through the activation of cannabinoid receptors (CB1 and CB2) in the central nervous system, which modulates neurotransmitter release and has been linked to cognitive impairment.45,46 However, the cognitive effects of cannabis appear to be influenced by tolerance, as frequent users develop resistance to its impact on cognitive function, while occasional users experience greater impairments.47,48 This may explain the lack of association with objective cognitive measures in our study, given that more than half of cannabis users (52.7%) reported frequent use (≥10 times) during the data collection period. Another possible explanation for our findings lies in the specific composition of cannabis used by participants. Cannabis products vary widely in their concentrations of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD), the two primary active cannabinoids. Previous research has shown that high-THC cannabis (e.g., Dronabinol) is associated with memory impairment, whereas cannabis with higher CBD content (e.g., Nabiximol) does not produce significant cognitive deficits.49,50 Nabiximols, a cannabis-based medication approved for treating spasticity in MS, has been demonstrated to have no detrimental effects on cognitive function in this population.51 While CBD has been found to mitigate the cognitive impairments associated with THC, it does not reduce psychotomimetic effects, as both high- and low-CBD cannabis have been associated with elevated symptoms of cognitive distortion.49 This may help explain our finding that cannabis use was associated only with greater perceived cognitive difficulties. Future research should consider not only the frequency and quantity of cannabis use but also the chemical composition of cannabinoid products consumed to better understand their impact on cognition in MS.
Nicotine and opioid use showed no significant within-person temporal associations with cognitive function. title: Dose-dependent effect of acute THC on extinction memory recall and fear renewal: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study.
abstract: Prior work from our lab and others demonstrates that the endocannabinoid system is a promising avenue for improving fear memory deficits in posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Specifically, 7.5 mg of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) decreases fear responding in healthy adults and increases prefrontal cortex activation during extinction learning and fear renewal in adults with PTSD. The present study will determine whether there is a dose-dependent effect of THC on short-term (24 h) and long-term (one week) fear learning and memory in adults with PTSD. Using a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled design, N = 36 adults with PTSD completed the study and were randomized to receive placebo (PBO, n = 11), 5 mg of THC (n = 11), or 10 mg of THC (n = 14) prior to fear extinction learning. Participants completed a Pavlovian conditioning paradigm with extinction recall and fear renewal occurring 24 h and one week later, where we measured concurrent functional imaging and behavioral responses. Twenty-four hours after drug administration, individuals with PTSD given 5 mg of THC exhibited greater anterior cingulate cortex and prefrontal cortex activation during early fear renewal. One week later, individuals given 10 mg of THC exhibited greater hippocampus activation during extinction recall and prefrontal cortex activation during fear renewal. These data suggest that dosing and timing are critical for facilitating fear memory processes in PTSD, and that low-dose oral THC prior to extinction learning can affect brain indices of fear learning and memory both acutely and one week after administration.

Introduction
Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a complex and debilitating mental health condition that can develop after exposure to a traumatic event (e.g., assault, motor vehicle accident, etc.; (American Psychiatric Association: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders 2013). First-line treatment for PTSD addresses its core dysfunction—poor extinction memory retention—via prolonged exposure therapy (Foa 2011). Exposure therapies rely on repeated presentation of trauma-related cues to promote extinction of fear and prevent renewal of fear (Foa et al. 2007). Despite their overall successes, nearly half of patients are left with lingering symptoms, due to poor extinction recall, or relapse within a year due to fear renewal (Foa et al. 1999; Hembree et al. 2003; Rothbaum et al. 2005). There is a great need to improve exposure therapy outcomes by (1) facilitating extinction learning and recall and (2) preventing later fear renewal.
Extinction of learned fear is dependent on the concerted effort of the amygdala and hippocampus to store the new, safe information that the event cue or reminder no longer predicts danger (Chhatwal et al. 2006; Ji and Maren 2007; Pape and Pare 2010). Extinction memory retention and recall, however, is primarily driven by the prefrontal cortex (PFC) and hippocampus (Berretta et al. 2005; Ji and Maren 2008; Milad and Quirk 2002; Paré and Smith 1993). In healthy humans, successful extinction memory recall is associated with hippocampus and vmPFC activation (Milad et al. 2007; Milad, Wright, Milad et al. 2007a, b). Adults with PTSD, however, have poor extinction memory retention and exhibit lesser activation of the PFC and hippocampus, and greater anterior cingulate cortex and amygdala activation, compared to healthy controls (Milad et al. 2008, 2009). Improving extinction retention and preventing fear renewal may therefore require pharmacological interventions that can target fear processes and their associated neural network.
Compelling evidence over the last two decades posits that the endocannabinoid (eCB) system is essential for extinction learning and recall. In rodents, blocking type-1 cannabinoid receptor (CB1R) transmission, the primary receptor of the eCB system, impairs fear extinction learning and later recall (Marsicano et al. 2002). Inhibiting the breakdown of eCBs, and therefore increasing eCB transmission and CB1R activation, improves fear extinction recall in rodents (Bitencourt et al. 2008; Chhatwal et al. 2005; Gunduz-Cinar et al. 2013; Pamplona et al. 2008). Systemic or intra-amygdala, -PFC, or -hippocampus administration of a CB1R agonist facilitates extinction learning and later recall (Kuhnert et al. 2013; Segev and Akirav 2011). In healthy humans, low dose, oral THC (7.5 mg) facilitates extinction recall and increases vmPFC and hippocampus activation during an extinction recall test (24 h later; (Rabinak et al. 2013, 2014). Likewise, we recently demonstrated that 7.5 mg THC increases vmPFC activation during extinction learning and 24 h later during fear renewal in adults with PTSD, compared to controls (Zabik et al. 2023). However, based on these data, it is unclear whether the dose used in prior studies (e.g., (Rabinak et al. 2013, 2014) is sufficient for maximizing gains related to extinction learning and retention, as well as preventing fear renewal.
To extend our prior work in adults with PTSD given low dose, oral THC, we report on a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to determine whether THC has a dose-dependent effect on extinction retention and fear renewal. Specifically, we aimed to determine whether increasing doses of THC in individuals with PTSD causes a linear, dose-dependent: (1) decrease in self-report measures of fear during a test of extinction recall or fear renewal and (2) increase in hippocampus and/or decrease in amygdala activation. Additionally, we determined whether the proposed effects would impact whole brain activation and be retained at a 1-week follow-up.
Materials & methods
Participants
Participants were recruited from the community via flyers, online postings, etc. (Detroit, MI) to complete a study testing the effects of a cannabinoid-based drug on fear memory in those with PTSD. Eligible participants were aged 18–60, right-handed, fluent in English, had at least a high school diploma or equivalent education, and had exposure to a Criterion A event defined by DSM-5 (detailed below). Participants were free of any MRI contraindications (e.g., ferrous metal in the body) and any neurocognitive impairment (including traumatic brain injury with current cognitive impairment). Participants who were pregnant or breast-feeding or were unable to tolerate small, enclosed spaces without anxiety (e.g., claustrophobia) were excluded. Participants with a current or past allergic or adverse reaction or known sensitivity to cannabinoid-like substances (dronabinol/marijuana/cannabis/THC, cannabinoid oil, sesame oil, gelatin, glycerin, and titanium dioxide) were also excluded from the study. Participants completed a novel, immersive reality Pavlovian fear conditioning paradigm that contained a snake stimulus; therefore, participants were screened for excessive fear of snakes (i.e., possible snake phobia) via the Snake Avoidance Questionnaire prior to participation (SNAQ; (Klorman et al. 1974). Potential participants with scores ≥ 24 on the SNAQ were excluded, following Fredrikson (Fredrikson 1983). All participants were required to test negative on a seven-panel urine drug screen and alcohol breathalyzer. Participants also could not have a psychotic or related disorder, could not pose a risk of harm to themselves or others, and could not be taking a medication with a level 1 (severe) drug-drug interaction with dronabinol.
In total, n = 139 participants were screened to complete the present study. Of those participants, n = 21 withdrew their consent, n = 28 were lost to follow-up prior to randomization, n = 23 were ineligible and did not complete the screening interview, n = 1 tested positive on a drug screen, n = 4 were not enrolled due to validity concerns with their interview. All participants completed the Life Events Checklist for DSM-5 to determine exposure to traumatic events in the participant’s lifetime (Weathers et al. 2013). A total of n = 62 participants endorsed a traumatic event that met Criterion A per DSM-5 criteria for PTSD (American Psychiatric Association: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders 2013). Of those that endorsed a Criterion A event, n = 44 met criteria for PTSD, by either meeting Clinician Administered PTSD Scale-5 (CAPS-5) diagnosis or having a total CAPS-5 severity score ≥ 25 (Weathers et al. 2018). Of note, the CAPS-5 is a structured interview designed to assess symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) according to DSM-5 criteria. It is considered the gold-standard for PTSD diagnosis and severity assessment. The n = 18 who did not meet these criteria were excluded from analyses. The CAPS-5 was administered by AI, CP, or NLZ after standardized CAPS-5 training with a licensed clinician; diagnoses were confirmed by CAR.
In addition to determining trauma exposure, psychiatric comorbidities were identified based on a computerized version (NetSCID-4, TeleSage) of the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (SCID-IV; (First et al. 2002) or the Mini International Neuropsychiatric Interview (MINI version 6.0.0; (Sheehan et al. 1998). Participants with a primary comorbid mood or anxiety disorder more debilitating and clinically salient than PTSD or with current substance or alcohol abuse or dependence were excluded; See Supplemental Data section S1.1 for more details. N = 44 adults met screening eligibility for PTSD and were randomized. Of those that met eligibility criteria, n = 8 were excluded, leaving N = 36. Reasons for exclusion include: lost to follow-up (n = 1) and incomplete functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data due to either technical errors or participant request to cease scanning (n = 7). See Fig. 1 for details about the recruitment pipeline.
The study protocols were approved by the Wayne State University Institutional Review Board, and all participants provided written informed consent prior to completing study procedures. Participants were compensated for their time. This study is a registered clinical trial investigating the effects of THC on fear extinction in participants with PTSD (NCT03008005).
Pavlovian conditioning paradigm
Participants underwent a well-validated, 3-day Pavlovian conditioning paradigm originally developed by Milad and colleagues (Milad et al. 2007). We previously reported on the modified version of this paradigm (Zabik et al. 2023; Zabik, Rabinak, Zabik et al. 2023a, b). Two different 3D environments consisting of different colors, textures, sounds (ambient noise related to context), and background scenes, constituted the contexts. The fear conditioning context (‘danger’ context, CXT + or A) is separate from the ‘safety’ context where fear is extinguished (CXT− or B). An extinction recall test occurs in the safety context (CXT−), while fear renewal occurs in the danger context (CXT+). The CSs were messenger bags in three colors of maximum discriminability for those with colorblindness. The unconditioned stimulus (US) was a 3D virtual snake darting out of a bag of a specific color [conditioned stimulus (CS); varying colors] and striking towards the participant’s point of view, paired with a snake hiss sound (800 ms, 50 dB, 60% reinforcement). This US was chosen as an evocative and ecologically threatening stimulus (Öhman 2005). Fear conditioning (~ 13.8 min) occurred outside the MRI scanner on a 24” LCD computer monitor in a standard lab office using a VR head-mounted Oculus Rift. They were presented with two CS + s (e.g., red bag and blue bag) that opened to reveal the snake and hissing sound during reinforced trials; in total, participants saw the bag for 4.5 s, where the final 0.8 s included presentation of the US. A third CS (e.g., yellow bag) was presented but never paired with the US (CS−); that is, the bag opened but no US occurred. CS + s had 8 non-reinforced presentations that were intermixed with an additional 12 presentations of each CS + that co-terminated with the US, and 20 presentations of the CS−. The next day, participants completed an extinction learning phase (~ 9.2 min) in the fMRI scanner. One CS + was presented in the absence of the US (CS + E, e.g., red bag). The other CS + was not presented (CS + U, e.g., blue bag). Extinction learning consisted of 20 CS + E and 20 CS − trials presented in the extinction context (CXT−; Fig. 2). Twenty-four hours later, participants returned to the MRI for an extinction recall test phase (~ 13.8 min) in CXT − and a fear renewal test phase (~ 13.8 min) in CXT+, where 20 presentations each of the CS + E, CS + U, and CS − were displayed. The US was not presented during extinction recall or fear renewal. One week later, participants returned to complete an additional test of extinction recall and fear renewal that was identical to the previous tests, which we denote as extinction recall or fear renewal ‘follow-up’. Fear extinction learning, extinction recall, and fear renewal were displayed using Vizard (WorldViz Version 5.0, WorldViz, Santa Barbara, CA, USA) on a screen viewed behind the scanner using a mirror affixed to the headcoil. Assignment of the CSs to the three colored bags was randomized for each participant. All stimuli were presented within the conditioning context (CXT+) during fear conditioning (Fig. 2). The designation of colored bags as CSs and the virtual environment as CXT + or CXT− was randomized across participants. The order of trials was also pseudo-randomized, so no more than 2 presentations of the same color bag occurred in a row.
Drug randomization and administration
Participants were randomized to receive an acute oral dose of THC (dronabinol, 5 or 10 mg capsule; Ascend Laboratories, LLC, Parsippany, NJ) or dextrose (PBO) using covariate adaptive randomization where a new participant was sequentially allocated to a drug group (PBO, 5 mg THC, 10 mg THC) by accounting for baseline characteristics (i.e., CAPS-5 total severity score, age, sex, and race). In this approach, the current distribution of participants across covariate is assessed and the marginal balance distance is calculated for each covariate to determine the imbalance between groups. The biased coin method with a probability of 0.7 was used to assign the next participant to the group that would minimize the imbalance. If both groups were equally balanced, then the participant was assigned to either group with a probability of 0.5 (Lin et al. 2015). The principal investigator (CAR) randomized participants, wherein participants and study personnel were blinded to the capsule content and drug group assignments.
Approximately 120 min prior to extinction learning, participants ingested a capsule of PBO (n = 11), 5 mg THC (n = 11), or 10 mg THC (n = 14). This administration corresponds to peak drug effects of orally ingested THC (Wachtel et al. 2002).
US expectancy ratings
Participants were instructed to rate (indicate) whether they thought they would encounter the US (see a snake popping out of the bag). Participants were instructed to make a rating of: “Yes, I do think [US] will occur”, “No, I do not think [US] will occur”, or “I don’t know”. This rating happened each time they saw the CS, as soon as they saw the CS. Responses were registered using a computer keyboard on Day 1 and an MR-compatible 4-button response device on Days 2 and 3.
Drug effects questionnaire
We collected data on subjective drug effects from participants during the drug day visit (Day 2) using the Drug Effects Questionnaire (DEQ; (Johanson and Uhlenhuth 1980). The DEQ included the following questions: (1) “Do you FEEL a drug effect right now?”, (2) “Are you HIGH right now?”, (3) “Do you DISLIKE any of the effects you are feeling right now?”, (4) “Do you LIKE any of the effects you are feeling right now?”, and (5) “Would you like MORE of the drug you took, right now?”. Participants rated their response on a 100 mm visual analog scale, from “not at all” to “extremely”. DEQ ratings were collected at baseline (prior to capsule administration) and at approximately 30, 60, 90, 180, and 240 min after capsule ingestion. We also collected DEQ ratings at approximately 120 and 150 min after capsule ingestion while participants were in the fMRI scanner.
Serum levels of THC
We collected blood plasma samples from participants on Day 2 (Extinction Learning) before and after they entered the MRI scanner. Serum samples were collected and processed as previously reported by Baglot and colleagues (Baglot et al. 2021). See Supplemental Information Section S1.1 for methodological details, and Section S2.3 for reported serum levels.
Functional imaging
Data collection and preprocessing
Blood-oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) fMRI data were collected from 66 axial, 2-mm-thick slices (set to the manufacturer-minimum gap size) using a T2*-sensitive gradient echo EPI acquisition sequence (repetition time = 2,000 ms; echo time = 30 ms; 128 × 128 × 66 matrix; field of view = 256 mm; flip angle = 73°; 2.0 × 2.0 × 2.0 mm voxels; multiband acceleration factor = 3). A T1-weighted anatomical image (repetition time = 1,820 ms; echo time = 3.52 ms; 256 × 256 × 120 matrix; field of view = 240 mm; flip angle = 8°; 0.94 × 0.94 × 1.5 mm voxels) and field map image (repetition time = 2,412 ms; echo time = 51 ms; 128 × 128 × 66 matrix; field of view = 256 mm; flip angle = 90°; multiband acceleration factor = 3) were collected within the same scan session for coregistration and distortion correction. Participants were inside the scanner for approximately 13 min prior to beginning the task to reduce the novelty of the scanning environment (5 min for T1-weight anatomical scan and 8 min for resting state).
FMRI data were analyzed using SPM8 software (Wellcome Department of Cognitive Neurology, London, UK; http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm). The following preprocessing steps were applied sequentially: (a) distortion correction, (b) realignment to first image, (c) slice timing correction, (d) coregistration, (e) normalization to MNI space, (f) reslicing, and (g) spatial smoothing (6-mm FWHM Gaussian kernel). Participants with high quality data and scan stability (minimum motion correction) were included in the analyses. See Supplemental Information Section S1.2 for details on motion-related quality control.
First-level model
After preprocessing, a general linear model was applied to the time series and convolved with the canonical hemodynamic response function (HRF) with a 128-s high-pass filter (Worsley and Friston 1995). Individual statistical parametric maps were calculated using this general linear model for each participant, for each condition type during fear extinction learning (CS + E, CS−) and extinction recall/fear renewal (CS + E, CS + U, CS−). To reduce the impact of motion-related artifacts, the following variables were included in the first-level model as nuisance regressors: the six movement parameters obtained during realignment, the derivatives of the movement parameters, and the quadratic terms for both the movement parameters and their derivatives. Volumes with excess motion (i.e., > 0.8 mm framewise displacement) were also added as nuisance regressors in the models.
Second-level model
First-level contrasts were submitted to second-level analyses in a random-effects statistical model in SPM8 (Friston et al. 1998). Previous animal work, as well as meta-analyses from human data, suggests that activation of fear-related brain regions is strongest during early phases of learning (e.g., extinction recall; see (Fullana et al. 2018; Milad et al. 2007b; Milad and Quirk 2002)). Therefore, fear extinction learning, extinction recall, and fear renewal were split into early and late, defined as the average of the first and second halves of each phase, respectively (10 trials per CS for early and 10 trials per CS for late).
Regions of interest (ROIs)
ROIs included anatomically defined bilateral amygdala and hippocampus, based on the AAL atlas (Tzourio-Mazoyer et al. 2002).
Whole brain analysis
In addition to small-volume, ROI-based analysis, we included whole-brain analyses in SPM12.
Statistical analyses
The primary focus of this study was to determine whether THC has dose-dependent effects on fear-related measures during Pavlovian conditioning in adults with PTSD, with a primary interest in short-erm (24 h) and long-term (1 week) extinction recall and fear renewal. Unless otherwise stated, data were analyzed using SPSS software (IBM SPSS Statistics 29).
US expectancy ratings
For analysis of US expectancy ratings, early fear conditioning is defined as the second trial, while early extinction learning, extinction recall, and fear renewal are defined as the first trials of each stimulus following prior work (Zabik et al. 2022; Zabik, Peters, Zabik et al. 2023a, b). Late trials for all phases are defined as the last trials of each stimulus per phase. Several stimuli had zero responses for a given category, likely due to small drug x trauma sample sizes. To address this issue for statistical analyses, we collapsed responses into two categories: ‘Yes/I don’t know’ and ‘No’.
During each phase, binary logistic regressions assessed the probability of participants responding ‘Yes/I don’t know’ vs. ‘No’. During fear conditioning, our aim was to validate that participants conditioned and differentiated between stimuli. We conducted time (early, late) x stimulus (CS + E, CS + U, CS−) binary logistic regression; we also conducted a prospective drug group (PBO, 5 mg, 10 mg) x time (early, late) x stimulus (CS + E, CS + U, CS−) binary logistic regression.
